fetched_contents.text: Newborn Screening Process This page features information about newborn screening (NBS) and what happens during each step in the process, including the 3 tests that are part of the screening process: blood spot screening, pulse oximetry screening, and hearing screening. Follow the links below for answers to commonly asked questions about NBS. * When Does NBS Happen? * Where does NBS Happen? * How Does NBS Happen? * Is NBS the Same for All Babies in the U.S.? * Before Newborn Screening: Questions to Ask When Does Newborn Screening Happen? The timing of newborn screening (NBS) is very important. Babies need screening during the first few days of life, because some of the conditions found by screening require treatment or intervention right away. NBS happens after birth, usually when your baby is between 24 and 48 hours (1 and 2 days) old. If a baby is tested before 24 hours, they may need to be retested. Some babies who have had treatments such as transfusions or dialysis may be tested later or may need further testing after their blood has returned to normal. In addition, babies who are born too early, or who receive nutrients or medicines before screening, may need further testing. There are two models that states use to screen all newborns: the one-screen model or the two-screen model. * Most states use the one-screen model. In this model, babies are screened only once when they are 24 to 48 hours old. This one screen looks for all conditions on the state’s newborn screening panel. * Thirteen states use the two-screen model. In this model, all babies are screened at 24 to 48 hours old and screened again at 1 to 2 weeks old. The second screen usually happens in a health care provider’s office as part of a well baby visit. * States choose the one-screen model or the two-screen model based on many factors. These factors can include historical practice in the state or the testing cut-offs (guidelines to decide if a baby needs follow up) the state uses. In either model, all babies are screened for all of the conditions that their state requires. * Whether you live in a one-screen or two-screen state, your baby may need additional screening and follow up based on their newborn screening results. To learn more about the differences in NBS across different states, visit the State pages. Where Does NBS Happen? All babies need NBS, regardless of where they are born. If your baby is born at a hospital, screening will happen before you take your baby home. Usually, a health care provider performs NBS in your room or a newborn/nursery area. If your baby has an out-of-hospital birth, screening can happen outside of the hospital like at your birth center or home. Many midwives are trained to complete NBS. If you are planning an out-of-hospital birth, talk to your midwife about NBS before your baby is born. If your midwife cannot perform NBS, make other arrangements. Your baby’s health care provider can help arrange screening by another midwife, a hospital, clinic, or local health department. It is important that you make a plan so your baby completes screening near the recommended age. How Does NBS Happen? Newborn screening has three different parts: 1. Blood spot screening, which determines if a baby might have one of many serious conditions 2. Pulse oximetry screening, which determines if a newborn might have certain heart conditions 3. Hearing screening, which determines if a newborn might be deaf or hard of hearing Blood Spot Screening Blood spot screening (sometimes called the “heel stick” or “24-hour test”) uses a few drops of blood from your baby’s heel to determine if your baby might have one of many serious conditions. Even though some health care providers still refer to blood spot screening as the “PKU test,” this term is no longer accurate because NBS now checks for many conditions. Following is a step-by-step guide explaining how blood spot screening happens: * Between 24 and 48 hours after birth, a health care provider will tell you that it is time for your newborn’s blood spot screening. * Your baby can stay swaddled during blood spot screening. * To make the process easier, the health care provider will gently warm your baby’s foot to increase blood flow. * The health care provider will then make a quick pinprick on your baby’s heel. Your baby may feel the prick and start to cry, but it will be over very quickly and will not leave a mark. * The health care provider will collect a few small drops of blood from your baby’s heel, then drop them onto small circles on a special card. * The part of the card with the circles contains a type of paper called filter paper. This paper absorbs the blood drops. * The other part of the card has information about your baby. This information tells whose blood is on the card and how to reach you and your baby’s health care provider. * Once the blood spots have dried, the card is sent off to a laboratory. There, the staff runs laboratory tests looking for signs of certain serious conditions. Each state has its own newborn screening panel, which is a list of the conditions that the state checks during NBS. To see the newborn screening panel for your state, visit the State pages. Results from blood spot screening are usually ready in about five to seven days. The public health laboratory sends your baby’s results to your baby’s health care provider, not straight to you. If the result suggests the presence of a condition, then either the health care provider or the state NBS program will contact you. Be sure to ask about your baby’s results at your baby’s first or second well-child visit. It is important to ask about your baby’s NBS results—do not assume that no news means that the results are in-range. To learn more about blood spot screening results, visit the Newborn Screening Results and Follow-Up page. ## Mini-report: core tests and what they screen for

Newborn screening panels are designed to detect disorders that are serious, potentially life-threatening, and often asymptomatic at birth. The evidence consistently identifies inherited metabolic disorders as the most common category targeted by newborn screening, along with endocrine disorders, hemoglobinopathies, immunodeficiency, cystic fibrosis, hearing loss, and critical congenital heart disease [N3-F2]. The standard newborn screening process uses a **dried blood spot test**, in which a few drops of blood are collected from the baby’s heel and placed on a filter paper card [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Specific metabolic disorders included in standard panels
The evidence points to a broad range of conditions, but it also emphasizes that the exact panel varies by country or region. In the U.S., the federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) provides a baseline, but states may expand or narrow it [N6-R2]. The search results list **PKU**, **hypothyroidism**, **galactosemia**, and **sickle cell disease** as examples of disorders included in common newborn screening panels [N1-R2]. The UpToDate overview also notes that screening panels can include many harmful and potentially fatal disorders that do not show signs or symptoms at birth [N1-R5]. Another source explicitly states that many states screen for **50 different disorders** [N3-R2], though the exact disorders are not enumerated in the excerpt.

### How each test is performed and what it detects
The dried blood spot test is the central method. It is performed **between 24 and 48 hours after birth**, usually by a health professional using a heel prick and collecting a few drops of blood onto a filter paper card [N3-F2]. The blood is then sent to a laboratory for analysis [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also describes a **two-screen model** in some U.S. states, where babies are tested once at 24–48 hours and again at 1–2 weeks [N5-F3]. The second screen is part of a well-baby visit and is intended to improve follow-up and detection [N5-F3].

### Universal versus condition-specific tests
The evidence shows a mix of universal and condition-specific coverage. In the U.S., all states have a public health program that screens babies for many serious conditions [N1-F1]. The federal RUSP provides a standardized baseline, but **each state has its own newborn screening panel** [N5-F3]. This means that the test is **universal in the sense that every baby is screened**, but the exact conditions included may vary by jurisdiction [N1-F1][N3-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that some conditions are included in the **RUSP** and thus are broadly adopted, while others may be added locally [N6-R2].

### Bottom line
Standard newborn screening panels are universal in most countries and regions, but the specific disorders included differ. The core test is the dried blood spot, performed by heel prick at 24–48 hours, and some states use a second screen later in the first week [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3]. The panel includes a broad set of serious disorders, especially metabolic, endocrine, and hemoglobinopathies, but not every jurisdiction screens for the same exact conditions [N1-R2][N3-F2][N6-R2].

## Mini-report: practical next steps and follow-up after screening

When newborn screening results are abnormal or inconclusive, the evidence indicates that **further testing is needed** before a diagnosis can be confirmed. The Minnesota Department of Health states that abnormal results may need additional tests to either clear or diagnose the baby [N4-R2]. The New England Consortium guide also notes that timely follow-up is important because abnormal results can indicate a metabolic disorder, and most repeat tests will be normal [N4-R3]. The UpToDate overview adds that abnormal results should prompt notification of the pediatric/primary care physician within 24–48 hours [N4-R4].

### What happens if results are abnormal or inconclusive
A positive result means the screening was abnormal and further testing is needed [N4-R2]. The evidence also describes a **false-positive result**, where the majority of repeat tests will be normal [N4-R3]. The Texas DSHS parent resources state that the doctor or staff member will contact parents if results are abnormal and further testing is required [N4-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that follow-up is important because abnormal results can indicate a metabolic disorder [N4-R1].

### When and how further testing or specialist referral is needed
The evidence suggests that follow-up is usually initiated quickly. Minnesota says newborn screening program staff will call parents if results are abnormal [N4-R2]. UpToDate says the pediatric/primary care physician should be notified within 24–48 hours after receipt of an abnormal screening result [N4-R4]. The Texas DSHS FAQ says the second newborn screen is completed between 7 and 14 days of age, and the program staff will contact parents if results are abnormal [N4-R1][N4-R5]. In other words, the family should expect a prompt follow-up call or communication from the screening program or the baby’s health provider.

### How families should respond to a positive result
Families should **not assume no news means no problem** [N5-F3]. They should ask about their baby’s results at the first or second well-child visit [N5-F3]. The evidence also stresses that results are usually ready in about five to seven days, and the public health laboratory sends results to the baby’s health care provider, not directly to the parents [N5-F3]. So the practical response is:  
1. **Wait for the result** and do not assume no news means no problem [N5-F3].  
2. **Ask the provider** about the results during the well-child visit [N5-F3].  
3. **Follow the provider’s instructions** for any repeat testing or specialist referral [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3].

### Bottom line
If screening results are abnormal or inconclusive, further testing is needed, and the majority of repeat tests are normal [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Families should ask the provider about results at the well-child visit and follow any follow-up instructions, because the result may indicate a serious disorder that requires treatment [N4-R1][N5-F3]. The process is designed to minimize false positives while ensuring timely intervention when a true disorder is suspected [N4-R3][N5-F3].

## Mini-report: mandatory versus optional screening and legal/health system context

Newborn screening is generally **legally required** in most countries and regions, but the exact legal structure and opt-out rules differ. The evidence states that in the United States and Canada, screening is **mandatory**, with an option for parents to **opt out in writing** if they desire [N2-R3]. It also notes that **nearly all states** in the U.S. require screening, although most allow parental refusals on religious and other grounds [N2-R5]. In contrast, the evidence indicates that screening is **not universally mandatory everywhere**—some countries and regions may not require it or may have less comprehensive coverage [N2-R1][N2-R4].

### Whether screening is legally required in the patient’s country or region
Because the patient’s country is not specified, the evidence can only summarize the general rule. In the U.S., screening is **required by state law** [N6-R5]. In Canada, the evidence says it is **mandatory** with an opt-out option [N2-R3]. In many other countries, the evidence suggests screening is **required in nearly all states** but may allow limited opt-outs [N2-R5]. However, the evidence also notes that some countries may not require screening and that screening can be **voluntary** in some contexts [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Which countries or regions require screening and which do not
The evidence does not provide a complete global list of all countries, but it does show a pattern. In the U.S., screening is **mandatory by state law** [N6-R5]. In Canada, screening is **mandatory** with an opt-out option [N2-R3]. In many developed countries, the routine screening panels include **20 or more disorders** [N2-R1]. In some countries, screening is **not required** or may be **targeted** [N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that **many countries** screen all newborns for PKU and hypothyroidism, but some may expand the panel more [N2-R1]. In Mexico and Latin America, the evidence says only metabolic NBS/ENBS involves molecular confirmatory testing, while other screenings are “merely” confirmatory [N2-R4], suggesting a mixed system rather than universal mandatory screening.

### Differences between universal coverage, voluntary, and targeted screening
The evidence supports a distinction between three models:
- **Universal coverage**: Screening is required for all newborns, usually by law or public health mandate. In the U.S., this is the standard; every state has a public health program that screens babies for many serious conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].
- **Voluntary screening**: Parents may choose not to participate, often with a written opt-out. In the U.S., this is allowed in nearly all states [N2-R5][N6-R4].
- **Targeted screening**: Screening is done only for certain conditions or only in certain settings. The evidence suggests that targeted screening may exist where panels are narrower or where confirmatory testing is used [N2-R4].

The evidence also indicates that some countries may have **mandatory screening** but **optional participation** in the sense that parents can opt out [N2-R3][N2-R5]. In contrast, **universal coverage** means all babies are screened regardless of parental preference, while **targeted screening** means not all babies are covered in the same way [N2-R1][N2-R4].

### Bottom line
Newborn screening is **mostly legally required** in most countries and regions, especially in the U.S. and Canada, but the exact legal requirement and opt-out rules vary [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R5]. In the U.S., screening is required by state law with an opt-out option [N6-R5]. In many other countries, screening is required in nearly all states but may allow limited refusals [N2-R5]. The system can therefore be described as a mix of **universal coverage**, **voluntary participation**, and **targeted or narrower screening** depending on the jurisdiction [N2-R1][N2-R4].

## Integrated patient answer: newborn metabolic screening tests, obligation, and next steps

If you have a newborn a few days old and want to know about tests for metabolic diseases, the short answer is: **yes, there is a standard newborn screening test for many serious metabolic and related disorders, and it is usually legally required in most countries, though the exact rules vary by place** [N2-R3][N6-R5][N1-F1].

---

## 1) What tests are used to screen for metabolic diseases?

Newborn screening is designed to detect serious conditions that can be life-threatening or cause long-term health problems before they become obvious [N3-F2]. The core test is the **dried blood spot test**, in which a few drops of blood are collected from the baby’s heel and placed on a filter paper card [N1-F1][N3-F2]. This blood sample is then sent to a laboratory for analysis [N3-F2].

### Which metabolic disorders are included?
The evidence shows that the panel varies by country or region, but a common pattern is broad coverage of **inherited metabolic disorders**, **endocrine disorders**, **hemoglobinopathies**, **immunodeficiency**, **cystic fibrosis**, **hearing loss**, and **critical congenital heart disease** [N3-F2]. Specific examples listed in the evidence include **PKU (phenylketonuria)**, **hypothyroidism**, **galactosemia**, and **sickle cell disease** [N1-R2]. The evidence also notes that many states screen for **50 different disorders** [N3-R2], though the exact list differs by jurisdiction [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### How the test is performed
The test is usually done **between 24 and 48 hours after birth**, often by a health professional using a heel prick [N3-F2][N5-F3]. In some U.S. states, a **second screen** is done later, usually at 1 to 2 weeks of age, as part of a well-baby visit [N5-F3]. The process is described as a **one-screen model** in most states and a **two-screen model** in thirteen states [N5-F3].

### Universal versus condition-specific tests
The test is **universal in most countries and regions**, meaning all babies are offered screening, but **not all panels are the same** [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In the U.S., each state has its own newborn screening panel, while the federal RUSP provides a baseline [N6-R2][N5-F3]. So the test is **universal in practice**, but the exact conditions included can differ locally [N3-F2][N6-R2].

- **Voluntary participation**: Parents may choose not to participate, often with a written opt-out. This is allowed in nearly all U.S. states [N2-R5][N6-R4].
- **Targeted screening**: Screening is done for only certain conditions or in only certain settings. The evidence suggests this may happen where panels are narrower or where confirmatory testing is used [N2-R4].

So if you are asking whether screening is **obligatory in your country**, the answer depends on where you live. If your country is **France, Canada, or the U.S.**, the evidence points to **mandatory screening with an opt-out option** [N2-R3][N6-R5]. If you are elsewhere, the evidence indicates screening is **usually required**, but the exact legal rule may differ [N2-R1][N2-R4].

## Mini-report: practical next steps and follow-up after screening

When newborn screening results are abnormal or inconclusive, the evidence indicates that **further testing is needed** before a diagnosis can be confirmed. The Minnesota Department of Health states that abnormal results may need additional tests to either clear or diagnose the baby [N4-R2]. The New England Consortium guide also notes that timely follow-up is important because abnormal results can indicate a metabolic disorder, and most repeat tests will be normal [N4-R3]. The UpToDate overview adds that abnormal results should prompt notification of the pediatric/primary care physician within 24–48 hours [N4-R4].

### What happens if results are abnormal or inconclusive
A positive result means the screening was abnormal and further testing is needed [N4-R2]. The evidence also describes a **false-positive result**, where the majority of repeat tests will be normal [N4-R3]. The Texas DSHS parent resources state that the doctor or staff member will contact parents if results are abnormal and further testing is required [N4-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that follow-up is important because abnormal results can indicate a metabolic disorder [N4-R1].

### When and how further testing or specialist referral is needed
The evidence suggests that follow-up is usually initiated quickly. Minnesota says newborn screening program staff will call parents if results are abnormal [N4-R2]. Families should **not assume no news means no problem** [N5-F3]. They should ask about their baby’s results at the first or second well-child visit [N5-F3]. If screening results are abnormal or inconclusive, further testing is needed, and the majority of repeat tests are normal [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Newborn screening is generally **legally required** in most countries and regions, but the exact legal structure and opt-out rules differ. ### Whether screening is legally required in the patient’s country or region
Because the patient’s country is not specified, the evidence can only summarize the general rule. In the U.S., screening is **required by state law** [N6-R5]. In Canada, the evidence says it is **mandatory** with an opt-out option [N2-R3]. In many other countries, the evidence suggests screening is **required in nearly all states** but may allow limited opt-outs [N2-R5]. However, the evidence also notes that some countries may not require screening and that screening can be **voluntary** in some contexts [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Which countries or regions require screening and which do not
The evidence does not provide a complete global list of all countries, but it does show a pattern. In the U.S., screening is **mandatory by state law** [N6-R5]. In Canada, screening is **mandatory** with an opt-out option [N2-R3]. In many developed countries, the routine screening panels include **20 or more disorders** [N2-R1]. The evidence supports a distinction between three models:
- **Universal coverage**: Screening is required for all newborns, usually by law or public health mandate. In the U.S., this is the standard; every state has a public health program that screens babies for many serious conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

The evidence also indicates that some countries may have **mandatory screening** but **optional participation** in the sense that parents can opt out [N2-R3][N2-R5]. In contrast, **universal coverage** means all babies are screened regardless of parental preference, while **targeted screening** means not all babies are covered in the same way [N2-R1][N2-R4].

### Bottom line
Newborn screening is **mostly legally required** in most countries and regions, especially in the U.S. and Canada, but the exact legal requirement and opt-out rules vary [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R5]. In the U.S., screening is required by state law with an opt-out option [N6-R5]. In many other countries, screening is required in nearly all states but may allow limited refusals [N2-R5].
